screens.title: Firebase Storage and Cloud Functions
screens.subtitle: Store user media, secure access, and run server-side logic without managing servers

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why Firebase Storage and Cloud Functions matter for mobile apps and how they work together. Firebase Storage gives you a scalable, managed place to keep user-generated files like profile pictures, videos, and documents. Cloud Functions provide serverless code that runs in response to events or HTTP requests, so you can offload heavy or sensitive work from the device. For example, upload an image from Flutter, then call a function to create a thumbnail or send a notification. You will see practical steps: enable Storage in the console, add the firebase_storage and image_picker packages, implement upload and download flows, apply Storage Security Rules to restrict access by user folder, and write and deploy simple Cloud Functions — both HTTP-triggered and event-triggered. We will also cover how to call functions from Flutter and common pitfalls like incorrect rules or missing billing for functions. By the end, you should be able to store files securely, trigger backend logic reliably, and integrate both into a Profile screen workflow. Reflect on this: what server-side tasks in your app belong on Cloud Functions rather than the client?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use Firebase Storage to manage files and Cloud Functions to run trusted server-side tasks that complement client behavior.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus your work on practical, verifiable skills. First, you will learn to upload and download files such as images and videos from a Flutter app using the firebase_storage package. That includes picking files, initiating an UploadTask, and retrieving a download URL. Second, you will be able to author and test Firebase Storage security rules so only authenticated users can upload and users can be restricted to their own folder — a critical step to prevent data leaks. Third, you will understand what Firebase Cloud Functions are and when to use them: for image processing, notifications, or integrating third-party APIs. Fourth, you will write and deploy a simple Cloud Function — HTTP-triggered or Firestore-triggered — and call it from Flutter. Each objective includes hands-on validation: uploading a profile picture, publishing secure rules, deploying a function, and invoking it from your app. These milestones align with real app requirements and help you move from prototype to a secure, maintainable implementation.

screens.title: What is Firebase Storage?
screens.subtitle: A managed object store for user-generated files

narration.text: Firebase Storage is a managed object storage service built on Google Cloud Storage. It stores binary objects — images, videos, documents — and serves them to clients while handling resumable uploads, retries, and large file transfer. In mobile apps this matters because you no longer need to build and maintain your own file server; Storage handles scale and network reliability. A concrete example is storing profile pictures: your Flutter app uploads an image, Firebase returns a download URL that your UI uses to show the picture. A common misconception is to treat Storage like a database; it is optimized for blobs and should not replace structured databases like Firestore for queryable data. Another frequent error is leaving default rules wide open during development, which exposes files to public access. Key takeaway: use Storage for files, keep metadata or references in Firestore if you need structured queries, and design folder paths that reflect ownership for secure rules. What file types will your app store, and where will metadata live? What is Firebase Storage? means firebase storage is a scalable, reliable object store for media and files used by mobile apps.. In practical terms, a managed object store for user-generated files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Firebase Storage is a scalable, reliable object store for media and files used by mobile apps.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What is Firebase Storage?
Definition

Managed object store built on Google Cloud Storage that handles file upload reliability and public URLs.

Why use it?
  • Scales automatically for user media.
  • Resumable uploads and retries reduce client complexity.
  • Works with Firebase Security Rules for access control.
Key Takeaway
Store binary files here, keep searchable metadata in Firestore. Design folder paths for secure rules.
Concrete example — Profile picture flow
User picks an image, app uploads with putFile, then stores the returned download URL with the user profile so the UI can display it.
Common misconception

Storage is not a queryable database. Avoid treating filenames as structured data; instead, store metadata in Firestore if you need queries or indexing.

screens.title: Enable Storage & set up packages
screens.subtitle: Console steps and Flutter dependency preparation

narration.text: Before writing code, enable Firebase Storage in the Firebase Console and prepare your Flutter project. In the console, go to Storage and click Get started, choose a default bucket location, and accept the initial settings. On the Flutter side, add the firebase_storage and image_picker dependencies to pubspec. yaml and run flutter pub get. This connects your app to Storage and gives you client APIs for picking files and uploading. A common mistake is to forget to configure firebase_core and authentication first — Storage operations usually assume an initialized Firebase app and, for secure uploads, an authenticated user. Example: after adding dependencies, initialize Firebase in main and ensure the current user is signed in before calling putFile. Key takeaway: enable Storage in the console, add required packages, and confirm initialization and auth status before attempting uploads. screens.title: Upload files from Flutter
screens.subtitle: Selecting a file, using putFile, and monitoring UploadTask

narration.text: Uploading from Flutter typically follows three steps: pick a file, create a storage reference, and call putFile to start the upload. The firebase_storage client returns an UploadTask which you can await or listen to for progress updates. A concrete example: use image_picker to let the user choose a photo, build a path like profile_pictures/{uid}/{timestamp}. jpg, then call ref. putFile(file). After the task completes, call getDownloadURL to obtain a URL to display or store. Watch for FirebaseException to handle failures. A common misconception is to assume putFile returns a URL immediately; it returns an UploadTask and you must await the TaskSnapshot before calling getDownloadURL. Also avoid deterministic filenames that collide; include a timestamp or unique id. Key takeaway: always monitor the UploadTask, handle errors, and then retrieve the download URL. Try a quick manual upload and verify the returned URL loads in your browser or emulator. Upload files from Flutter means pick file → ref.child(path) → putfile(file) → await task → snapshot.ref.getdownloadurl().. In practical terms, selecting a file, using putfile, and monitoring uploadtask. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Upload pattern
keyIdea.text: Pick file → ref.child(path) → putFile(file) → await task → snapshot.ref.getDownloadURL().

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Upload files
Code walkthrough: uploadProfilePicture()
import 'dart:io';
import 'package:firebase_storage/firebase_storage.dart';
import 'package:image_picker/image_picker.dart';
import 'package:firebase_auth/firebase_auth.dart';

final FirebaseStorage _storage = FirebaseStorage.instance;
final ImagePicker _picker = ImagePicker();

Future uploadProfilePicture() async {
  final User? currentUser = FirebaseAuth.instance.currentUser;
  if (currentUser == null) return null;

  final XFile? image = await _picker.pickImage(source: ImageSource.gallery);
  if (image == null) return null;

  File file = File(image.path);
  String fileName = 'profile_pictures/${currentUser.uid}/${DateTime.now().millisecondsSinceEpoch}.jpg';
  Reference ref = _storage.ref().child(fileName);

  try {
    UploadTask uploadTask = ref.putFile(file);
    TaskSnapshot snapshot = await uploadTask;
    String downloadUrl = await snapshot.ref.getDownloadURL();
    return downloadUrl;
  } on FirebaseException catch (e) {
    return null;
  }
}
Explanation & example
  • Use image_picker to let the user choose an image file from the gallery or camera.
  • Create a unique path with the user's uid and a timestamp to avoid filename collisions.
  • Await the UploadTask and then call getDownloadURL to obtain a usable URL.
Common mistake

Calling getDownloadURL before the upload completes or using non-unique filenames can return stale URLs or overwrite files.

Check your understanding

How will you ensure uploaded files don't collide and how will you report progress to the user?

screens.title: Monitor progress and download files
screens.subtitle: Track uploads and retrieve file URLs for display or storage

narration.text: Monitoring upload progress improves UX by showing progress indicators and handling retries. The UploadTask returned by putFile exposes snapshot events and a TaskSnapshot you can await to get final state. In Flutter you can listen to uploadTask. snapshotEvents to update a progress bar using bytesTransferred and totalBytes. After completion, call snapshot. ref. getDownloadURL to get the public URL. For downloads, one approach is to use the download URL with an HTTP client or let the platform image loader fetch the URL directly. The provided downloadFile example prints the URL and notes that you can use the http package to actually fetch the bytes and save them locally. Misconception: a download URL is not permanent if you later change security rules—if you need persistent public access, consider a proper public folder, but balance that with privacy needs. Key takeaway: present progress to users, await completion before using URLs, and plan where to store returned URLs for easy retrieval. Monitor progress and download files means listen to uploadtask.snapshotevents for progress, await the final snapshot, then call getdownloadurl to use the file.. In practical terms, track uploads and retrieve file urls for display or storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Listen to UploadTask.snapshotEvents for progress, await the final snapshot, then call getDownloadURL to use the file.

Monitor UploadTask

Subscribe to snapshotEvents to compute percentage progress and update a progress bar in your UI.

// Example listener
uploadTask.snapshotEvents.listen((TaskSnapshot snapshot) {
  final progress = snapshot.bytesTransferred / snapshot.totalBytes;
  // update progress bar with progress value
});
After await uploadTask, call snapshot.ref.getDownloadURL() and store that URL with your user record in Firestore or Auth profile.
Download considerations
  • Use the returned download URL directly in image widgets if rules allow public reads.
  • For private files, you may use authenticated requests to fetch bytes and save locally.
  • Store URLs persistently unless you will regenerate them later.

screens.title: ProfileScreen implementation walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Connect Storage operations to your app UI and user profile

narration.text: This guided walkthrough shows how a ProfileScreen ties together Storage uploads, user state, and UI feedback. The screen loads the current user's photoURL if available, or lists Storage items in a profile_pictures folder to find a default image. On upload, it sets an isUploading flag, uses image_picker to select a file, stores it with a unique path that includes the user ID and timestamp, awaits the UploadTask, retrieves the download URL, updates the user's photoURL, and reloads the user to reflect changes. Error handling reports upload failures to the user. A common misconception is to rely solely on Storage listing to find a user's photo; instead store the returned URL in Firestore or the user's Auth profile to simplify retrieval. Key takeaway: centralize the URL in a single authoritative place in your app so UI loads reliably. Consider how you will handle multiple files per user and what naming scheme keeps lookups simple. ProfileScreen implementation walkthrough means update the user's profile with the download url after a successful upload and use it as the single source of truth for the displayed image.. Essential behavior

  2. Pick an image and set an uploading flag to show a spinner.
  3. Upload to profile_pictures/{uid}/{timestamp}.jpg and await the task.
  4. Get download URL and update the user's profile with updatePhotoURL.

String downloadUrl = await snapshot.ref.getDownloadURL();
await currentUser.updatePhotoURL(downloadUrl);
await currentUser.reload();
setState(() { _profileImageUrl = downloadUrl; _isUploading = false; });
Show success feedback and handle FirebaseException to surface errors to the user via SnackBar or inline error messages.

screens.title: Storage Security Rules
screens.subtitle: Control who can read and write files in your bucket

narration.text: Storage Security Rules determine who can upload, download, and delete files. Rules use path matching like match /profile_pictures/{userId}/{fileName} and conditions that inspect request. auth. A common pattern is to allow read and write only when request. auth is not null and request. auth. uid equals the userId path segment — this prevents users from accessing other people's files. Another pattern is to expose a public folder for images meant to be widely accessible while restricting uploads to authenticated users. A frequent and dangerous mistake is leaving default rules too permissive during development. Always publish restrictive rules and only open specific paths intentionally. Example rules in the source enforce per-user access for profile_pictures and a public_images folder with read access for anyone but write only for authenticated users. Key takeaway: design folder structure first, then write precise match rules that reflect ownership and purpose to reduce accidental exposure and unexpected billing. Storage Security Rules means write path-specific rules that require request.auth and match request.auth.uid to the userid path segment for ownership-based access.. In practical terms, control who can read and write files in your bucket. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security first
keyIdea.text: Write path-specific rules that require request.auth and match request.auth.uid to the userId path segment for ownership-based access.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Storage Security Rules
Example rules
rules_version = '2';
service firebase.storage {
  match /b/{bucket}/o {
    match /profile_pictures/{userId}/{fileName} {
      allow read, write: if request.auth != null && request.auth.uid == userId;
    }

    match /public_images/{fileName} {
      allow read: true;
      allow write: if request.auth != null;
    }

    match /{allPaths=**} {
      allow read, write: if false;
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • The profile_pictures rule enforces ownership by matching the path userId to request.auth.uid.
  • public_images is readable by anyone but writable only by authenticated users.
  • The catch-all denies access to paths not explicitly matched.
Common mistake

Publishing permissive rules early can expose user data and allow malicious uploads that increase billing. Always test and then restrict rules before release.

screens.title: Common mistakes & best practices
screens.subtitle: Security, storage structure, and billing pitfalls

narration.text: There are recurring pitfalls when combining Storage and Cloud Functions. One risk is leaving Storage rules open; an exposed bucket can leak private files and allow arbitrary uploads that incur costs. Another is relying on file listings instead of storing a canonical download URL with the user's profile — listings are brittle and slower. For Cloud Functions, forgetting to enable billing on a Blaze plan prevents functions from deploying or running in certain cases. A misconception is thinking functions always run for free; some triggers or outbound integrations require a billing-enabled project. Best practices: design folder paths that reflect ownership, store metadata and canonical URLs in Firestore or Auth profiles, publish restrictive rules with explicit match paths, and enable billing only when you intend to use functions that require it. Also limit function permissions and monitor logs for unexpected activity. Key takeaway: combine secure rules, explicit metadata storage, and billing awareness to keep costs and risks under control. Common mistakes & best practices means avoid permissive rules, rely on canonical urls for retrieval, and enable billing only when required for cloud functions.. In practical terms, security, storage structure, and billing pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls to avoid
keyIdea.text: Avoid permissive rules, rely on canonical URLs for retrieval, and enable billing only when required for Cloud Functions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Mistakes & Practices
Mistakes
  • Leaving Storage rules permissive during development.
  • Using file listings as the primary way to find a user's photo.
  • Not enabling billing when functions require Blaze plan, causing deployment failures.
Best practices
  • Store canonical download URLs in user records in Firestore or Auth profile.
  • Use path-based rules that match ownership and deny by default.
  • Monitor function logs and set quotas to avoid unexpected billing.
Check question

Which folder paths will you create and what rule will enforce ownership for each?

screens.title: What are Firebase Cloud Functions?
screens.subtitle: Serverless Node.js functions triggered by events or HTTP

narration.text: Firebase Cloud Functions let you run backend code in response to Firebase events or HTTP requests without provisioning servers. They are written using Node. js and are useful when client-side code is inappropriate — for example, resizing images, sending push notifications, or performing secure server-side validation. A concrete example: when a new message document is added to a chat collection, a Firestore-triggered function can run to send a push notification or add a server timestamp. Misconception: Cloud Functions are not a replacement for a full backend when you need persistent long-running processes. They are best for short-lived event handlers and APIs. Remember that some features require billing to be enabled and that runtime versions must match supported Node. js versions. Key takeaway: use Cloud Functions to run trusted logic securely and to offload heavy processing from client devices. What are Firebase Cloud Functions? means serverless code that reacts to events or http calls to perform backend work you don't want on the client.. In practical terms, serverless node.js functions triggered by events or http. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cloud Functions
keyIdea.text: Serverless code that reacts to events or HTTP calls to perform backend work you don't want on the client.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Cloud Functions
Concept

Functions run in a managed Node.js environment and can be triggered by Firebase features like Firestore, Storage, Auth, or via HTTP. They are ideal for operations that must run on a trusted backend.

Use cases
  • Send push notifications when a new message arrives.
  • Resize uploaded images after Storage onFinalize events.
  • Perform server-side validation or aggregation after Firestore writes.
Limitations & checks
  • Not for long-running background processes; prefer other compute options when needed.
  • Check billing plan requirements for certain triggers and networking features.
  • Monitor logs with the Firebase Console to diagnose failures.

screens.title: HTTP-triggered Cloud Function example
screens.subtitle: Write, initialize, and deploy a simple function callable from Flutter

narration.text: An HTTP-triggered function is a simple way to provide a custom endpoint your app can call. Initialize a functions project with the Firebase CLI and choose JavaScript or TypeScript. The example greetUser function logs a message and responds with plain text. To deploy, run firebase deploy --only functions from the functions directory. In Flutter you can call the endpoint with an HTTP GET or use the cloud_functions package for callable functions which handle auth automatically. Misconception: don't embed secret keys or sensitive logic on the client and expect the function to secure it — move that logic entirely into the function. Also remember to test functions locally with the emulator before deploying. Key takeaway: HTTP functions create custom APIs for Flutter apps; deploy them with the CLI and call them with an HTTP client or callable wrapper for secure integration. HTTP-triggered Cloud Function example means create an https.onrequest function, deploy it with the firebase cli, and call it from your flutter app using an http client or callable wrapper.. In practical terms, write, initialize, and deploy a simple function callable from flutter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: HTTP function
keyIdea.text: Create an https.onRequest function, deploy it with the Firebase CLI, and call it from your Flutter app using an HTTP client or callable wrapper.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › HTTP Cloud Function
functions/index.js
const functions = require('firebase-functions');

exports.helloWorld = functions.https.onRequest((request, response) => {
  functions.logger.info("Hello logs!", {structuredData: true});
  response.send("Hello from Firebase!");
});
Deploy with firebase deploy --only functions. After deployment, use the console to find the function URL and call it from your app or the browser to verify it responds.
Calling from Flutter
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

Future callHelloWorldFunction() async {
  final String functionUrl = 'YOUR_CLOUD_FUNCTION_HTTP_URL';
  final response = await http.get(Uri.parse(functionUrl));
  if (response.statusCode == 200) {
    print('Cloud Function response: ${response.body}');
  }
}
Or use FirebaseFunctions.instance.httpsCallable for callable functions that manage auth context automatically.

screens.title: Event-triggered function: image processing example
screens.subtitle: Use Storage triggers to process uploads, e.g., generate thumbnails

narration.text: Event-triggered Cloud Functions let you run code automatically when a Storage object changes. A common use case is generating thumbnails when users upload images. The function listens for onFinalize on storage. object, checks content type to ensure it is an image, and skips files already in a thumbnail folder. It downloads the uploaded image, uses an image processing library such as sharp to resize it, and uploads the thumbnail back to Storage. This moves heavy C P U work off the mobile client and centralizes processing. Misconception: assuming the trigger will run instantly in all cases; there may be slight delays and you should design idempotent functions and checks to avoid repeated work. Also ensure your functions runtime and dependencies are supported. Key takeaway: use onFinalize triggers to reliably run server-side processing after uploads and upload results back to Storage or update Firestore references accordingly. Event-triggered function: image processing example means use storage.object().onfinalize to run server-side processing like thumbnail generation automatically after uploads.. In practical terms, use storage triggers to process uploads, e.g., generate thumbnails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event trigger
keyIdea.text: Use storage.object().onFinalize to run server-side processing like thumbnail generation automatically after uploads.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Storage trigger
Thumbnail generator (conceptual example)
exports.generateThumbnail = functions.storage.object().onFinalize(async (object) => {
  const fileBucket = object.bucket;
  const filePath = object.name;
  const contentType = object.contentType;

  if (!filePath || object.resourceState === 'not_exists' || !contentType.startsWith('image/')) {
    return null;
  }
  if (filePath.startsWith('thumbnails/')) return null;

  const bucket = admin.storage().bucket(fileBucket);
  const file = bucket.file(filePath);
  const thumbnailFilePath = `thumbnails/${filePath.split('/').pop()}`;
  const thumbnailFile = bucket.file(thumbnailFilePath);

  const [imageBuffer] = await file.download();
  const resizedBuffer = await sharp(imageBuffer).resize(200,200).toBuffer();
  await thumbnailFile.save(resizedBuffer, { contentType });
  return null;
});
Test with the emulator or a staging project, ensure the function skips thumbnails and handles non-image uploads safely. Log actions for observability.

screens.title: Call Cloud Functions from Flutter
screens.subtitle: Use callable functions or HTTP requests with authentication

narration.text: You can call Cloud Functions from Flutter two main ways: HTTP requests to an exposed URL or callable functions that automatically include the user's auth context. For callable functions add cloud_functions to pubspec and use FirebaseFunctions. instance. httpsCallable('functionName') to call a function and receive structured JSON. For simple HTTP endpoints, the http package works fine. Handle errors by catching FirebaseFunctionsException or HTTP errors and showing appropriate messages. Example: a greetUser callable function returns a greeting message and throws an unauthenticated error if the call lacks auth. Misconception: expecting callable functions to bypass security; callable functions still enforce server-side checks and can throw HttpsError values to signal auth or validation issues. Key takeaway: prefer callable functions when you need the Firebase auth context automatically; use plain HTTP when you expose a public A P I or need custom headers. Call Cloud Functions from Flutter means use httpscallable for auth-aware calls and http.get/post for simple public endpoints; handle exceptions and show clear ui feedback.. In practical terms, use callable functions or http requests with authentication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calling functions
keyIdea.text: Use httpsCallable for auth-aware calls and http.get/post for simple public endpoints; handle exceptions and show clear UI feedback.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Call Functions
Callable function (Flutter)
import 'package:cloud_functions/cloud_functions.dart';

Future _callGreetUserFunction() async {
  final HttpsCallable callable = FirebaseFunctions.instance.httpsCallable('greetUser');
  final result = await callable.call>({'name': 'user@example.com'});
  print('Function result: ${result.data?['message']}');
}
HTTP call (Flutter)
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

final response = await http.get(Uri.parse('YOUR_CLOUD_FUNCTION_HTTP_URL'));
if (response.statusCode == 200) {
  print(response.body);
}
Handle FirebaseFunctionsException for callable functions to present friendly error messages for auth and validation issues.

narration.text: These three concepts capture the chapter's core. First, Firebase Storage is the managed object store for app media; store binary files here and keep searchable metadata in Firestore or the Auth profile. Second, Storage Security Rules must be path-specific and ownership-aware; require request. auth and test rules to avoid accidental public access. Third, Firebase Cloud Functions provide server-side execution for HTTP or event-driven tasks like thumbnail generation or sending notifications; deploy via the Firebase CLI and call from Flutter using callable or HTTP endpoints. A common thread is designing your folder layouts and data flow so security and retrieval are simple. Keep URLs and metadata authoritative in one location and prefer serverless functions for trusted, heavy, or sensitive operations. Which of these concepts will you apply first in your project?

Third, use Cloud Functions for tasks clients should not or cannot perform: resizing images, sending notifications, or integrating with third-party services.
